header: IN THE PESHAWARHIGH COURT, BANNU BENCH, BANNU
Mr. Inam Ullah Khan Maxwat, Advocate (via
body: AURANGZEB. J,- Through this appeal under Section 96(1), C.P.C., the appellant has called in question the judgment and decree dated 19.L1.2O25, passed by the learned trial Court in Civil Suit No. 12/l of 2025, whereby his suitwas dismissed.

2. The brief facts, as emerging from the record, are that the appellant instituted a suit against the respondents seeking rendition of accounts amounting to Rs. 100,000,000/-, recovery of thirteen oil tankers altegedly belonging to the Marwat Group, possession of an inherited residential house, recovery of motor vehicle bearing registration No.AI(Z-969, Model 2OO7, allegedly valued at Rs. 1 ,500,000/ -, and a decree for permanent injunction. The appellant asserted that he had initially carried on business in partnership with his brothers, which partnership was dissolved during the years 2OIO-2O11, whereafter he continued the business in his individual capacity. He further asserted that the business and its assets included landed property measuring 02 kanals and 07 marlas and 08 kanals and 19 marlas, besides three houses/ bungalows.

3. According to the appellalt, respondents No.l to 5, being his sons, were initially engaged by him on a salaried basis and were subsequently entrusted with the management of the business and its accounts. He alleged that, taking advantage of the trust reposed in them, they misappropriated the business assets, excluded him from its affairs and deprived him of his lawful share and property. He further alleged that an amount of Rs.18,000,000/- was transferred by respondents No. 1 to 5, without his consent or authority, to respondent No.6, In-charge Manager of an Attock Petroleum ftlling station situated near Chaklala Air Base, Rawalpindi, on interest basis. The appellant also asserted that, despite his efforts to resolve the dispute through the Dispute Resolution Council (DRC), Lakki Marwat, the matter could not be settled.

4. The respondents were summoned through ordinary process as well as publication in the daily newspaper "Ausaf', Islamabad. Despite service, they did not appear before the learned trial Court and were proceeded against ex parte. The learned trial Court thereafter directed the appellant to produce evidence in support of his claim. The appellant appeared as PW-l on 14.10.2025 and produced documentary evidence, including Ex.PW-1/1, comprising 31 pages relating to the Marwat Group; Ex.PW-L12, the decision of the DRC; Ex.PW-1/3, Fard Jamabandi for the year 2Ol3-2O14; arrd Ex.PW- 1/4, the plaint. Upon conclusion of the proceedings, the learned trial Court dismissed the suit through judgment and decree dated 19.1 1.2025, principally observing that the appellant had failed to produce sufficient documentary evidence to establish ownership of the oil tankers, houses and motor vehicle. It also observed that the Fard Jamabandi had not been produced through proper authorised custody.

5. Learned counsel for the appellant contended that the impugned judgment is contrary to law and the evidence available on record. It was argued that, despite the respondents having been duly served and proceeded against ex parte, the learned trial Court failed to properly examine and appreciate the statement of the appellant and the documents produced by him. It was further contended that the suit was dismissed without a meaningful examination of the distinct claims and reliefs sought by the appellant and without recording adequate reasons for rejecting the evidence. No one appeared on behalf of the respondents to controvert these submissions.
6. I have heard learned counsel for the appellant and examined the available record with his assistance.

7 . The principal question requiring determination is whether, after proceeding ex parte against the respondents and recording the appellant's statement and documentary evidence, the learned trial Court properly evaluated the material on record and decided the controversy in accordance with law.

8. Order IX Rule 6, C.P.C., deals with the procedure to be adopted where the plaintiff appears but the defendant does not appear when the suit is called on for hearing. The relevant provision reads as follows:

Procedure when only plaiatiff appears.-( 1) Where the plaintiff appears and the defendant does not appear when the suit is called on for hearing, then- (a) When summons duly served. If it is proved that the summons was duly served, the Court may proceed ex parte and pass decree without recording evidence;
(b) When summons not duly served. If it is not proved that the summons was duly served, the Court shall direct a second summons to be issued and served on the defendant;

(c) When summons served, but not in due time. If it is proved that the summons was served on the defendant, but not in sufficient time to enable him to appear and answer on the day fxed in the summons, the Court shall postpone the hearing of the suit to a future day to be fixed by the Court, and shall direct notice of such day to be given to the defendant."

A plain reading of the above provision shows that, where the Court is satisfied that summons has been duly served and the defendant nevertheless fails to appear, it may proceed ex parte and is legally empowered to pass a decree even without recording evidence' The use of the word umay'' confers discretion upon the Court, which must be exercised judicially in the light of the circumstances of the case and the nature of the relief claimed. The provision does not mal<e the grant of a decree automatic upon the defendant's non-appearance' nor does it entitle the plaintiff to every relief claimed merely because the defendant has failed to contest the proceedings.

9. In the present case, the learned trial Court did not pass a decree without recording evidence under Order IX Rule 6(l)(a), C.P.C. Rather, it directed the appellant to produce evidence in support of his claim. The appellant accordingly appeared as PW-l and produced documents exhibited as Ex.PW-1/ I to Ex.PW- I

14. The learned trial Court thereafter adjudicated the suit on the basis of the statement and documentary material produced by the appellant and dismissed it on the ground of insufficiency of evidence. Having elected to record evidence, the Court was required to examine and evaluate that evidence in its proper perspective and give reasons for accepting or rejecting it. The respondents' absence did not relieve the appellant of his burden to prove the case; equally, it did not absolve the Court of its duty to assess the evidence brought on record.

10. ln Munautar Ahmed. Chtef Edltor Dallu Sama and. anotler v. Muhammad f and others IPLD 2O27 Suoreme Court 564. the august Supreme Court repelled the contention that an ex parte decree must follow merely because the defendant had not appeared to rebut the ptaintifl's claim. It was held that, even where the defendants are proceeded against ex parte, the Court is required to exercise its discretion judicially and examine the worth and credibility of each item of the plaintiffs claim before accepting or rejecting it. The Court emphasised that an ex parte decree cannot be granted mechanically by accepting the plaintifl's claim in toto, particularly where the claim is unsupported by evidence. The principle laid down squarely applies to the controversy before this Court. It reinforces the obligation ofthe trial Court to scrutinise each distinct relief and the evidence tendered in its support, rather than either accepting the claim automatically or rejecting it through a general observation regarding insufficiency of evidence.

11. In Fede of Po.k throuoh retattt. Mln of Defence. Rautalptndt and o;notlter u. Jlfiessrs Farttkh Internatlonal lhtt. Ltd. t h its r 12O23 SCMR 1119. tJre august Supreme Court considered the scope of Order IX Rule 6, C.P.C., in conjunction with the definition of a decree under Section 2(21, C.P.C. The Court recognised the discretion available to a trial Court to proceed ex parte and pass a decree without recording evidence, while emphasising that the exercise of such discretion must be judicial and consistent with the requirements of the administration of justice. Similarly, in Ghulam Alt Shah and others v. Murtamma.d Nhalid and others 12017 SCMR 78491. the august Supreme Court reiterated that a plaintiff must succeed on the strength of his own case and that the defendant's nonappearance neither discharges the plaintiffs burden of proof nor creates an automatic presumption in his favour. Thus, even in ex parte proceedings, the Court is required to determine the plaintifl's entitlement on the basis of the pleadings and evidence available on record.

12. The next aspect relates to the framing of issues. Order XIV Rule 1(6), C.P.C., provides an exception to the ordinary requirement of framing and recording issues where the defendant, at the first hearing ofthe suit, makes no defence. The relevant provision reads: "(6) Nothing in this rule requires the Court to frame and record issues where the defendant at the first hearing of the suit makes no defence."

The provision dispenses with the formal exercise of framing issues in the circumstances specified therein. Consequently, the mere omission to frame formal issues in a case where the defendant makes no defence at the first hearing cannot, by itself, be treated as sufficient to invalidate the proceedings. However, such dispensation does not absolve the Court of its obligation to identify the material questions arising from the plaintifl's case and determine them in accordalce with law. The absence of a contesting defendant may dispense with formal issues, but it does not dispense with judicial scrutiny of the claim and the evidence produced in its support.

13. The requirement of a reasoned judgment is expressly embodied in Order XX Rule 4(2), C.P.C., which provides: "(2) Judgments of other Courts. Judgments of other Courts shall contain a concise statement of the case, the points for determination, the decision thereon, and the reasons for such decision."
Likewise, Order XX Rule 5, C.P.C., provides:

"5. Court to state its decision on each issue. In suits in which issues have been framed, the Court shall state its finding or decision, with the reasons therefor, upon each separate issue, unless the finding upon any one or more of the issues is sufficient for the decision of the suit." A combined reading of these provisions makes it clear that a judgment must disclose the controversy before the Court, the material questions requiring determination, the conclusions reached and the reasons supporting those conclusions. Where issues have been framed, findings with reasons are required on each separate issue, subject to the exception contained in Rule 5. Even where formal issues are not required under Order XIV Rule 1(6), the Court must still identify and determine the material questions arising from the case in a reasoned manner.

14. In the present case, the appellant sought several distinct reliefs, including rendition of accounts, recovery of thirteen oil tankers, possession of an inherited residential house, recovery of tJre motor vehicle bearing registration No.AllZ-969 and permanent injunction. These claims were founded upon different factual assertions and required consideration in the light of the evidence relevant to each. The claim for rendition of accounts required examination of the alleged business arrangement, the entrustment of management and accounts to respondents No.l to 5, and the alleged exclusion of the appellant from the business affairs. Similarly, the claims relating to the oil tankers, landed property, residential houses and motor vehicle required examination of the appellant's asserted ownership, title, possession or other legal entitlement, as the case may be.

15. A perusal of the impugned judgment shows that the learned trial Court dismissed the suit mainly on the ground that the appellant had not produced sufficient documentar5r evidence to establish ownership of the oil tankers, houses and motor vehicle. It also questioned the manner in which the Fard Jamabandi had been produced. However, the judgment does not reflect a sufficiently structured examination of the documentary evidence, particularly Ex.PW- 1/ 1 and Ex.PtN -l 12, nor does it disclose a separate assessment of the material questions relating to the different reliefs claimed by the appellant. The learned trial Court was required to examine the statement of PW-l in conjunction with the documents produced by him and determine their relevance, admissibility and evidentiary value. Their mere exhibition did not establish the truth of every assertion contained therein; nevertheless, their contents and legal signilicance required consideration before the claims could be rejected.

16. The same was true of Ex.PW-1/3, the Fard Jamabandi for the year 2013-2014. If the learned trial Court considered that the document had not been produced through proper authorised custody or that its evidentiary value was otherwise deficient, it was required to record a clear {inding supported by relevant legal and factual reasons. The claims relating to the oil tankers, residential property and motor vehicle likewise required examination in the light of the evidence produced. The burden of proving the foundational facts remained upon the appellant in terms of Articles 117 and 118 of tlle Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984. However, the Court was required to determine whether that burden had been discharged by evaluating the evidence and recording reasons for its conclusion.

17. It is also significant that the claim for rendition of accounts stood on a different footing from the claims for recovery of specific movable and immovable property. The former required consideration of the alleged business relationship, the entrustment of management and accounts, the transactions allegedly undertaken by the respondents and the appellant's entiflement to seek rendition of accounts. The latter required determination of the appellant's asserted ownership or other legal entitlement to the specilic properties. The learned trial Court was, therefore, required to examine the nature and legal basis of each relief separately. A general observation regarding insufficiency of documentary evidence, without an adequate discussion of the material questions and the evidence relating to them, does not satisfy the requirement of a reasoned adjudication under Order XX Rule 4(2]., C.P.C.

18. A judgment is the culmination of judicial proceedings and must demonstrate that the Court has applied its mind to the pleadings, evidence and applicable law. This obligation is not diminished merely because tJre proceedings have been conducted ex parte. The Court is not bound to accept the plaintiffs assertions in the absence of the defendant; nevertheless, where evidence has been recorded, it must evaluate that evidence ald explain whether the plaintiff has established the essential ingredients of his claim. The impugned judgment, in its present form, does not sufficiently demonstrate such an exercise in respect of the distinct reliefs sought by the appellant.

19. The question now arises as to the appropriate course to be adopted by this Court in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction. Section 107, C.P.C., confers upon an appellate Court the power to determine a case finally, remand it, frame issues and refer them for trial, or take additional evidence or require such evidence to be taken. The provision reads:
Powers of Appellate Court.{1) Subject to such conditions and limitations as may be prescribed, an Appellate Court shall have power- (a) to determine a case frnally;
(b) to remand a case;
(c) to frame issues and refer them for trial;
(d) to take additional evidence or to require such evidence to be taken.

(2) Subject as aforesaid, the Appellate Court shall have the same powers and shall perform as nearly as may be the same duties as are conferred and imposed by this Code on Courts of original jurisdiction in respect of suits instituted therein."

20. Order XLI Rule 23, C.P.C., provides for remand where the Court from whose decree an appeal is preferred has disposed of the suit upon a preliminary point and the decree is reversed in appeal. Since the suit in the present case was dismissed after recording evidence and not upon a preliminary point, the conditions of Rule 23 are not attracted. Order XLI Rule 24, C.P.C., enables the appellate Court to determine the case finally where the evidence on record is sufficient to pronounce judgment, after resettling the issues, if necessary. On the other hand, Order XLI Rule 25, C.P.C., provides a mechanism for framing and referring an omitted issue or question of fact essential to the decision of the suit to the trial Court for determination, while the appeal remains pending before the appellate Court.

27Lt, ln Hablb tllbh o. Azmat Ulah |PLD 2007 remc CourA the august Supreme Court considered the scope of the appellate powers under Order XLI Rules 23,24 and 25, C.P.C., and emphasised that remand should not be ordered as a matter of routine. Where the evidence is sufficient, the appellate Court should endeavour to determine the case finally under Rule 24, whereas Rule 25 provides an appropriate course for obtaining hndings on omitted issues or questions of fact. The appellate Court is, therefore, required to examine the nature of the defect in the judgment and the state of the record before selecting the appropriate course. The power of remand under Section lO7, C.P.C., must likewise be exercised judicially and in accordance with the scheme and limitations of the Code.

22. Applyrng the above principles to the facts of the present case, I am of the view that the controversy cannot appropriately be determined finally by this Court under Order XLI Rule 24, C.P.C. Tlre impugned judgment does not contain an adequate evaluation of the evidence and the distinct claims raised by the appellant. The available record, therefore, does not provide a sufficient basis for this Court to record linal findings on all the matters in controversy. Likewise, a limited reference under Order XLI Rule 25, C.P.C., would not adequately address the deficiencies noticed, as the omission is not confined to one isolated issue or question of fact. The suit involves several substantive claims requiring examination of the pleadings, identification of the material questions, assessment of the oral and documentary evidence and determination of the appellant's entitlement to each relief. In these circumstances, this Court considers it appropriate to exercise its appellate jurisdiction under Section 107, C.P.C., and remit the matter to the learned trial Court for fresh adjudication in accordance with law, so that the entire controversy may be examined in its proper perspective and a reasoned decision may be rendered on each relief claimed.

23. For the foregoing reasons, this appeal is allowed. The judgment and decree dated 19.11.2025, passed by the learned trial Court in Civil Suit No.12/ I of 2025, are set aside, and the case is remanded to the learned trial Court for fresh decision in accordance wittr law. The learned trial Court shall examine the pleadings, the statement of PW-l and the documents already produced, including Ex.PW- 1/ 1 to Ex.PW- 1/4, identify the material questions arising l0 from the controversy and determine each relief claimed by the appellant separately. The admissibility, relevance and evidentiary value of the documents shall be assessed in accordance with law, and the appellant shall remain under the obligation to establish his claims in terms of the applicable law of evidence. The learned trial Court shall not treat the respondents' non-appearance as an automatic admission of the appellant's claims and shall decide the suit through a speaking judgment in conformity with Order XX Rule 4(21, C.P.C. The remand shall not be construed as an unrestricted permission to fill any lacuna in the evidence or to introduce further material, except as permitted by law. The parties shall be afforded an opportunity of hearing in accordance with law, and the suit shall preferably be decided within six months from the receipt of the record.

24. Needless to observe that the observations made herein are confined to the procedural and legal deficiencies noticed in the impugned judgment and shall not prejudice the learned trial Court while deciding tJle suit afresh on its own merits. The learned trial Court shall independently assess the evidence and record its findings in accordance with law.
The record of the trial Court be sent back forthwith along with a copy of this judgment.
